hints: Remember you are given the template strand, not the coding strand, so do not match the DNA letters directly to the mRNA stop codons. Ask yourself what DNA template bases would pair with UAA, UAG and UGA during transcription.

Use complementary base pairing for transcription (DNA A with RNA U, DNA T with RNA A, DNA C with RNA G, DNA G with RNA C) to work out the three DNA template triplets that make a stop, then look for the option that creates one of these from a non-stop triplet.
walkthrough:
**Work backwards from mRNA to DNA template**

Think like RNA polymerase. It reads the template strand and builds mRNA by complementary pairing.

Remember the pairing rules for transcription:
$$DNA\ A \rightarrow RNA\ U, \quad DNA\ T \rightarrow RNA\ A, \quad DNA\ C \rightarrow RNA\ G, \quad DNA\ G \rightarrow RNA\ C$$

**Find the three template triplets for stop**

Now apply that to the three stop codons:
$$UAA \text{ comes from template } ATT$$
$$UAG \text{ comes from template } ATC$$
$$UGA \text{ comes from template } ACT$$
So a premature stop means a mutation must CREATE one of ATT, ATC or ACT.

**Test each mutation for a new stop**

Look for a change from a normal codon to a stop template.

In option C, template ACC would make mRNA UGG (tryptophan, a normal amino acid), but mutated template ATT would make mRNA UAA (stop). That is a new stop signal in the middle of the message, so translation stops early.

options.A: Both ATT (UAA) and ATC (UAG) are already template triplets for stop codons, so this is a stop to stop change, not the creation of a new premature stop.
options.B: ACT makes mRNA UGA (stop) but ACA makes mRNA UGU (cysteine), so this mutation removes a stop rather than creating one.
options.C: ACC makes mRNA UGG (normal amino acid) but ATT makes mRNA UAA (stop), so this creates a new premature stop codon.
options.D: ATC makes mRNA UAG (stop) but TAG makes mRNA AUC (isoleucine), so this mutation removes a stop rather than creating one.
